summary: This October 13, 2023 news feature challenges the 'Automation Apocalypse' narrative, arguing that automation and AI will mostly transform rather than eliminate jobs. Experts quoted argue that technology has historically created new sectors, that cobots augment human work, and that reskilling and inclusive policy are key to a smooth transition. It also acknowledges risks of deepening socio-economic divides if access to new jobs is not inclusive.
one_line: A news feature argues automation will reshape rather than end work, stressing augmentation, reskilling, and inclusive policy over fears of mass unemployment.
key_facts: The article is dated October 13, 2023 and challenges the 'Automation Apocalypse' narrative of a jobless dystopia.

Amanda Chen, analyst for the Tech Future Council, spoke at the annual Work and Learn Conference in Boston last September, arguing history shows technology creates jobs in new sectors, not just displacement.
Technology ethicist Rick Sanderson says 'there is a distinct difference between repetitive tasks and holistic jobs.'
Self-checkout machines are ubiquitous, yet personal shopping assistants, custom tailoring experts, and culinary artists remain in high demand.
Cobots, or collaborative robots, work alongside humans to boost productivity; industrial psychologist Mariah Watkins stresses the empowerment they bring.
Economist Julian Ford says unemployment numbers need context, since rates fluctuate due to market trends, consumer behavior, and technological disruption.
The gig economy has exploded and is described as a redefinition of work rather than a crisis.
Google and Amazon have launched initiatives to train employees in high-demand tech skills.
Renewable energy, biotech, and cyber-security are expected to see significant job growth.

Entrepreneur and investor Leo Martinez argues automation lays the groundwork for a 'creative renaissance' and compares future new jobs to social media managers and app developers created by the internet era.
Policy consultant Aisha Thompson warns of deepening socio-economic divides without inclusive access to new digital-age jobs.
The article concludes that the operative term should be 'augmentation' rather than substitution, urging informed optimism.
